title: This Isnt an Academic School
author: Caiti Wade
source: The Disruptive Educator (Caiti Wade Substack), February 9, 2026
summary: Wade pushes back on the recurring claim 'not all schools are focused on academics, so evidence-based instruction isn't really relevant here,' arguing that this implies the purpose of high-quality teaching is league-table prestige rather than student learning. Drawing on her own life — a hardship-scholarship move to a private school during a period of family instability that gave her teachers' high expectations and consistent structures, which made school her safe place — she frames evidence-based practice as fundamentally about students, not metrics. She acknowledges schools using best practice tend to show up in those metrics, but treats that as a side effect: behind every good test result are individual students supported to learn as well as they could, especially those who would otherwise lean on private tutors and external resources their classmates cannot access. Wade pairs this with a synergy claim about wellbeing: in trauma-and-instability settings, explicit predictable instruction reduces emotional load and is one of the most supportive things a school can offer, not a competitor to wellbeing. The piece's sharpest move is naming the alternative as 'disadvantage by design': a school's choice to opt out of high-quality instruction is not a neutral contextual adjustment but a decision about which students get access to teaching that opens future pathways and which students do not, and the consequences fall hardest on the kids without compensating outside support.
points: Saying 'not all schools are academic' implies evidence-based practice exists to optimise league-table outcomes for schools rather than learning for students; the argument doesn't hold once you separate the side effect (better metrics) from the purpose (each student learning).

Behind every headline test score are individual students given consistent explicit teaching that maximised their chances; absence of such teaching pushes the work onto private tutors and outside resources, which not all families can access.

Wellbeing and best practice are synergistic, not competing: explicit predictable instruction in trauma-affected settings reduces mental and emotional load by giving students predictability, which is itself protective.
Highly structured classrooms are calm and orderly, not cold or uncaring; they let students focus their energy on learning rather than navigating uncertainty.

Opting out of evidence-based instruction is not a neutral contextual choice — it's disadvantage by design, because it limits which students access the knowledge, skills, and post-school pathways that high-quality teaching opens.
quotes: Buried within this argument is the implication that the primary purpose of high-quality instruction is improved performance on rankings, school league tables, or whatever public measure of academic prestige exists in your area. It implies that evidence-based practice exists to optimise outcomes for schools, rather than learning for students.
Behind every good end of school score, standardised test result, or headline-worthy outcome are several individual students who were supported to learn as well as they possibly could.

Crucially, it meant students were getting what they needed in the classroom. That is, not having to rely on private tutors, external support or family resources, that we know not all students have access to, to fill the gaps later. That's what evidence-based instruction does when it's done well.

Prioritising wellbeing doesn't mean instruction becomes optional. In fact, explicit, evidence-based instruction can be one of the most supportive things we offer students in those settings. When there are clear lesson structures, predictable expectations and familiar instructional techniques, students know what's coming.
Highly structured classrooms aren't cold or uncaring. They're calm and orderly. They allow students to focus their energy on learning, rather than navigating uncertainty.

If we accept that some schools 'aren't academic', then we quietly accept that the students in those schools don't require, or perhaps, don't deserve, the same quality of instruction as their peers in another school. And that's a position worth interrogating.

Students with access to tutors, resources and support outside of school might find ways to compensate. Students without those supports don't get that option. For them, the classroom is the opportunity. By deciding that a school isn't 'academic' and therefore shouldn't implement best practice, it's not a harmless contextual adjustment. That's a decision about which students get access to high-quality teaching, and which don't. That's disadvantage by design.” Archived from The Disruptive Educator (Caiti Wade Substack) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
